**Surah ash-Shams**

It is a Meccan surah without any disagreement, and its verses number sixteen according to the Meccan and the first Medinan count, and fifteen according to the others. When Allah, glory be to Him, concluded the previous surah with mention of the people of the right hand (*ashab al-maymanah*) and the people of the left hand (*ashab al-mash'amah*), He repeated both groups in this surah by way of a summary (*fadhlakah*), saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies it﴾ and ﴿And he has certainly failed who instills it [with corruption]﴾. In this surah it is: ﴿And inspired it [with] its wickedness and its righteousness﴾. This is like an explanation of His saying, exalted is He, in the first surah: ﴿And We guided him to the two ways﴾, according to the first of the two interpretations. Allah, glory be to Him, concluded the first surah with some of the conditions of the disbelievers in the Hereafter, and He, mighty and majestic, concludes this one with some of their conditions in this world. So the Mighty Speaker says:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾, meaning its light, as al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from Ibn 'Abbas. The intended meaning is when it rises and its authority is established.

Some of the verifying scholars (*muhaqqiqun*) said: The real meaning of *duha* (brightness) is the sun's distance from the visible eastern horizon and its appearing to observers, and then it became the term for that time. Thereafter, the first part of the time is called *dahwah*, what follows it is called *duha*, and what comes after that until near midday is called *dihaa'* with a fatha and a long alif. When it is attributed to the sun, it is a metaphor for its shining, as here. It is reported from al-Mubarrad that *duha* is derived from *dhibb* (ضِحّ), which is the light of the sun, and that the alif is transposed from the second *ha'* (ح), and likewise the waw of *dahwah* is transposed from it. Abu Hayyan responded to him, saying: Perhaps this is a fabrication against him, because al-Mubarrad is too great to go in this direction, and these are two different roots, one of which cannot be derived from the other. It has been answered that he did not reject minor derivation (*al-ishtiqaq al-saghir*), and his position is not hidden from the young or the old. From Muqatil: *duhaha* means its heat, which is explanation by a necessary consequence. And from Muqatil: the intended meaning is the entire day, and in this view, Allah swore by it shortly after that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 91, verse 2:

﴿By the moon when it follows it﴾. That is, it follows it (tabi'aha). It has been said: this is with regard to its rising and the sun's rising, i.e., when its rising follows the sun's rising, by rising from the eastern horizon after the sun has risen. That is at the beginning of the month, for when the sun rises from the eastern horizon at the start of the day, the moon rises after it, but without any authority (sultan), so it is seen after the sun sets as a crescent (hilal). The relevance of this to the oath by it is that it describes it by the beginning of its matter; just as the forenoon is the youth of the day, so the first sighting of the month is like its birth. It has also been said: this is with regard to its rising and the sun's setting, i.e., when its rising follows the sun's setting. That is on the night of the full moon, the fourteenth of the month, for then it is opposite the sun, and the distance between them is half the orbit of the sphere. When the sun is in the upper half of it, namely that which is above our heads, the moon is in its lower half, namely that which is beneath our feet; so when the sun sets, the moon rises from the eastern horizon. This is what is narrated from Qatadah. As for their saying that it is called badr (full moon) because its rising precedes the setting of the sun, so that it is like the sun's "badr" (its early counterpart) in rising, this does not contradict it, because that is based on approximation. The relevance of this to the oath by it is that it is the time of the manifestation of its authority, which fits the glorification of its status. Ibn Zayd said: it follows the sun throughout the whole month; in the first half it follows it by rising, and in the second half by setting, and his meaning is what has been mentioned in the two opinions. It has also been said: the intended meaning is that it follows it in illumination, by rising and appearing luminous at the sun's setting, taking its light from it; and this is in the first half of the month, for in it the moon takes a certain amount of light each night, unlike the second half. This is narrated from Ibn Salam, and al-Zamakhshari chose it.

Al-Hasan and al-Farra' said, as in al-Bahr: that is, it follows it at every time, because it receives light from it, so it follows it for this reason. Some people denied that any of the early scholars held that the light of the moon is derived from the light of the sun, and claimed that this is merely the opinion of the astrologers. What has been mentioned is an argument against him, and the proof for the basic question is clearer than the sun itself: namely, the variation of its light-forms by nearness and distance from it, together with the disappearance of its light when the earth comes between it and the sun. As for the variation being due to the possibility that one of its halves is luminous while the other half is not, and that it rotates on its axis with a rotational motion so that each half is seen gradually, and as for the disappearance of light at the interposition being due to the possibility of a dense body coming between us and it which we do not see, these are weaker than spider's threads, as is not hidden. Al-Zajjaj and others said: ﴿تَلاها﴾ means it became full and round, so it was following the sun in roundness and perfection of light.

By the day when it displays it (the sun).

Al-Alusi's commentary:

﴿By the day when it displays it﴾. That is: the day displays the sun; i.e., it makes it manifest, for the sun becomes clear and visible when the day has spread out and a period of it has passed. The attribution is therefore metaphorical (majazi), like the attribution in the phrase: "he fasted his day" (ṣāma nahārahu). It has also been said: the object pronoun refers to the earth; and it has been said: it refers to the world (al-dunya), by which is meant the surface of the earth and what is upon it. And it has been said: it refers to the darkness, and "jallāhā" then means "removed it" (azālahā). The non-mention of the referent (al-marji') in these opinions is because it is known. The first opinion is preferable, because the referent is mentioned and the pronouns are consistent (ittisāq al-ḍamā'ir). Some have permitted that the hidden subject pronoun in "jallāhā" refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as though it were said: "and by the day when Allah, exalted is He, displays the sun", so that He, glorified is He, would have sworn by the day in its most perfect state. And that, as you see, is far-fetched.

[p. 142]

﴿By the night when it covers it﴾: that is, the sun, so that it covers its light. The attribution (al-isnad, the ascribing of the act to the night) is as it was explained earlier. It has also been said: that is, the earth. And it has been said: that is, the world (al-dunya).

Here the present tense is used instead of the past, as in the previous verse, so that it would be said "when it covered it." Abu Hayyan said: "For the sake of the verse-ending (al-fasila, the rhyming close of the verse), and he did not say 'ghasshaha' (the intensive past form), because that would require omitting one of the two objects, since it is transitive to both. It is said: 'ghashiyathu kadha' (it covered him with such-and-such), as al-Raghib said." That is what has been said.

One of the eminent scholars said: the present tense is used to alert to the equality of times in His sight, glorified is His majesty.

Al-Khafaji said: "The first (view) is that by the night is meant the darkness that arises from the absence of light, not the original non-existence and the original darkness, for this is more evident in indicating power, and it is in the future relative to what precedes it, so the expression must be changed to indicate the intended meaning."

Al-Zamakhshari found the matter difficult regarding the accusative (nasb) of "idha" (when), because if the letters other than the first waw are conjunctive (atifa), it would entail conjunction onto two objects (ma'mulayn) of two different governing elements (amilayn), like conjoining "the day," for example, onto "the sun," which is the object of the oath particle; and conjoining the adverb, namely "idha" in ﴿when it displays it﴾, onto its counterpart in ﴿when it follows it﴾, which is the object of the oath verb. And if they are oath-particles, it would entail the gathering of multiple sworn items upon one answer (jawab), and al-Khalil and Sibawayh disliked this. He answered by choosing the first option and negating what it entailed, saying: the oath waw has the peculiarity that the verb is entirely omitted with it, unlike the ba' (the oath particle "bi"), with which the verb sometimes appears and sometimes is elided. So the waw stands in the place of the oath verb, and its ba' serves in the place of both together. The conjunctive waws are substitutes for this oath waw, so they govern the genitive (jarr) and govern the accusative (nasb). Thus the conjunction is of the kind of conjoining onto the objects of a single governing element, as you say: "Zayd struck 'Amr, and Bakr (struck) Khalid." So you put it in the nominative by the waw and in the accusative because it stands in the place of "struck," which is its governing element. End of quotation.

You know that the first of the conjunctive waws here has nothing with it that governs the accusative. Perhaps he meant that they govern that if there is an accusative object, or that they govern in the sense that the meaning of ﴿and the sun and its brightness﴾ is "and the sun and its light when it shines." Also, no one has said that the conjunctive particles are governing elements. Furthermore, the problem is based on the impossibility of conjoining onto the objects of two governing elements absolutely, even though some scholars permit it absolutely or on condition that the conjoined item is genitive, as in your saying: "In the house is Zayd, and in the room 'Amr." There would be no problem then. Also, it is based on accepting this objection and on the impossibility of escaping the gathering (of oaths) by positing an answer for each of the sworn items; if this is not accepted, or it is accepted and an answer is posited for each answer, no problem remains.

Also, it is based on the premise that "idha" is temporal (zarfiyya), and this is disputed, since it may be that it has been stripped of its temporal sense, in which case it would be a substitute (badal) for what follows the waw, as has been said regarding his statement:

"And after tomorrow, alas for my soul, from a tomorrow when my companions depart and I am not one who departs."

Here "idha" is a substitute for "ghad" (tomorrow). Even if we grant that it is temporal, it is permissible to posit with each (sworn item) a governed noun (mudaf) on which it depends, as if one posited "and the following of the moon when it follows it, and the revealing of the day when it reveals it, and the covering of the night when it covers it"; or to make it dependent on an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial (hal) element posited before what follows it; that is: "He swore by the moon being at the time when it follows it, and by the night being at the time when it reveals it," as one of them claimed. In this there is discussion.

Also, what applies to al-Zamakhshari is something like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿By the night when it turns away﴾ ﴿and by the dawn when it breathes﴾, because the waw there is conjunctive, and the explicit oath verb has already preceded, as Shaykh Ibn al-Hajib mentioned. Moreover, the verification, as some verifiers said, is that the adverb is not an object of the oath verb, because the meaning is corrupted; for restricting by time is not intended, whether in the present or the future. Rather, it is the object of a posited governed noun of the type "greatness," since swearing by a thing is magnifying it; so it is as if He swore by the greatness of such-and-such a time. As for what has been objected to this, that His swearing by a thing is a borrowing to show His greatness and to make clear His nobility, so it is permissible to restrict it by reference to a part of the intended meaning, namely the showing; and furthermore, if swearing is magnifying, positing it becomes idle. Even if this is granted, the figure of speech is either a subordinate metaphor (tab'iyya) or a representational one (tamthiliyya). In any case, there is nothing that, by the rules of grammar and the posited supposition, would be dependent on it so that what is intended from it, emphasized, would become evident; therefore there is no idle element.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 91, verse 5–6:

﴿Wa-as-samā'i wa-mā banāhā﴾ — i.e., "and by Him who built it" (wa-man banāhā). The use of "mā" (what) instead of "man" (who), in order to indicate the attribute (al-wasfiyyah), magnifies [the Subject] compared with what preceded in ﴿wa-mā walad﴾ (and what he begot). It is as if it were said: "by the Mighty One of great station who built it." His building of the two (the heaven and the earth) indicates His existence and the perfection of His power. What is meant by "building" is bringing it into existence in such a way that it points to this and can be used as evidence for Him. This is preferable to interpreting it as "its Builder" (bāniyhā), because it conveys the intended meaning of "building" (al-binā'). The same applies to the words of the Exalted: ﴿wa-al-arḍi wa-mā ṭaḥāhā﴾ — i.e., He spread it out on every side and made it level (wa-waṭṭa'ahā), (and) "kadahā" (He made it smooth). Here ṭaḥā means "went" (dhahaba), as in the verse of ʿAlqamah:

Ṭaḥā bika qalbun fī al-ḥisān ṭarūbu, bu'ayda al-shabābi ʿaṣrun ḥāna mashību
(A heart was led astray by you, longing for the beautiful women, after youth, an age of greying has come.)

And it means "rose high and ascended" (ashraqa wa-irtafaʿa). Among their oaths: "No, by the moon when it rises" (lā wa-al-qamari al-ṭāḥī). It is said: ṭaḥā yaṭḥū ṭaḥwan, and ṭaḥā yuṭḥī ṭaḥyan.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 91, verses 7–8:

His statement, glorified is He: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾. That is: He brought it into being and originated it, prepared for its perfection; and that is by the balancing of its limbs and its powers, both the outward and the inward. The indefiniteness (of nafs, "soul") is for magnification, and it has been said that it is for glorification, on the basis that the intended "soul" is Adam, peace be upon him. The first (view) is more fitting to the answer of the oath that comes later. Whoever holds that view makes this an instance of istikhdam (a figure of speech in which one word is used in two senses).

Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, al-Mubarrad, Qatadah and others held that "ma" (in "wa ma sawwaha") in the three places is a verbal noun (masdariyyah), that is: and its construction, and its spreading out, and its proportioning. Al-Zamakhshari objected to this, saying that it is not the correct reading, because of the Almighty's statement: ﴿Then He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾, and because of what it leads to of corruption of the composition; and this is according to what is in the marginal notes (al-Hawashi), because of what it entails: the coordination of a verb upon a noun, and that it would have no subject, neither an apparent one, which is evident, nor a pronoun, for lack of a referent. It was objected that the last point is refuted by the preceding verbs, namely "He built it, He spread it out, He proportioned it," and that the indication of context is sufficient for the validity of the pronoun. As for the first point, the coordination of a verb upon a noun is not corrupt, although it is contrary to the apparent sense; moreover, it applies to what follows "ma," as if it were said: "And a soul, and its proportioning, and then its inspiring with its wickedness and its piety." This was objected to on the ground that the fa' indicates sequence without interval, while the proportioning occurs before the breathing of the spirit and the inspiration occurs after puberty. It was answered that proportioning is the balancing of the limbs and powers, among which is the faculty of thought, and inspiration is an expression for explaining how they are to be used in the two paths in this place; it is not separate from it since it was proportioned, and it does increase according to the increase of the powers, in mode but not in existence. Moreover, the interval in such cases is customary, and it may be considered consecutive without delay. Furthermore, the objection applies equally to both views. There is no sense in al-Tibi's statement: "The secret structure requires conformity of the parallel clauses, so it is not permissible; (to say) 'a soul and its proportioning, then Allah inspired it' would make it already attained; and that is only based on the supposition that His statement ﴿then He inspired it﴾ is a full clause, and with a full clause the corruption of this view does not appear."

Qadi Abd al-Jabbar insisted only on the masdariyyah and not the relative (mawsuliyyah) reading, saying: "Because of what would follow from it: the placing of an oath by other than Allah before His oath by Himself, glorified and exalted is He."

The Imam answered this by saying that the greatest of perceptible things is the sun, so Allah mentioned it together with its four attributes which indicate its greatness; then the Most Holy Essence mentioned Himself and described Himself, majestic and exalted, with three attributes, so that the intellect might be enabled to grasp the majesty and greatness of Allah, glorified is He, as befits Him, and the senses do not contest it. Thus this was a means of drawing the intellect from the depths of the world of perceptible things to the wide expanse of the height of His grandeur, exalted is His majesty. It is also permitted that "ma" be an expression for the matter for which the heaven was built, the earth was spread out, and the soul was proportioned, namely the countless wisdoms and benefits; and the attribution of the verbs to it would then be metaphorical. The subject of "alhamaha" (He inspired it) may be that matter, and the attribution would also be metaphorical; this, as you see, is (far-fetched).

As for wickedness (fujur) and piety (taqwa), according to what Abd ibn Humayd and others narrated from al-Dahhak, they are disobedience and obedience in general, whether they are of the heart or of the body. Their inspiring to the soul, according to what he and Ibn Jarir and a group narrated from Mujahid, is their making the soul know them so that it distinguishes its right guidance from its error; this is also narrated from Ibn Abbas, as in al-Bahr. Close to this is the saying of Ibn Zayd: "He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety" meaning, He made them clear to it.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated something similar from Qatadah. On this view the verse is similar to His statement: ﴿And We guided him to the two paths﴾. Wickedness was placed before piety because its inspiration in this sense is among the beginnings of avoiding it, and that is takhliyah (emptying, clearing away), and takhliyah precedes tahliyah (adorning). It has also been said that it was placed first for the sake of the rhyme (fawasil). The two were attributed to the pronoun of the soul; it has been said that this indicates that what is inspired into the soul is wickedness and piety, for which it has been prepared, so they belong to it by virtue of that preparation. It has also been said that this is for the sake of the rhyme as well.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 91, verse 9–10:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he has succeeded who purifies it﴾ is the response to the oath, according to what al-Jama'ah narrated from Qatadah, and al-Zajjaj and others went to this view. The omission of the lam (lam al-qasam) is frequent, especially when the speech is long, which calls for lightening, or for the lam being replaced by what stands in its place. The subject of ﴿zakkaha﴾ is the pronoun of "man" (man), and the object pronoun refers to the soul (nafs). The same applies to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he has failed who corrupts it﴾. The repetition of "qad" (indeed) in it serves to display the concern for affirming its content and to signal that the oath is essentially connected to it. Al-tazkiyah (purification) is growth (al-tanmiyah), and al-taddsiyah (corruption) is concealment (al-ikhfa'). The original form of dassa is dassasa, and the third of the identical letters was changed into a ya', then it was changed into an alif because it is vowelled and the letter before it is open. Some of them spoke in general terms and said: a letter of weakness (harf 'illah) was substituted for that, as they said in taqaddada, taqadda, and dassasa (for intensification) in dassa, meaning "concealed." The poet said:

"You buried Amr in the dust, so his widows became widowed orphans, neglected."

In al-Kashshaf: al-tazkiyah is growth and elevation, and al-taddsiyah is diminishment and concealment; that is: he has indeed won every desired thing and been saved from every disliked thing, who makes his soul grow and elevates it through piety, in knowledge and action; and he has indeed lost, who diminishes it and conceals it through wickedness
صفحة 144
in ignorance and transgression.

It is also permitted to interpret al-tazkiyah as purification from the filth of matter (al-hayula), and al-taddsiyah as concealment within it and being soiled by it. In any case, in the promise and the threat mentioned, together with His swearing by what He swore by, there is an indication of knowledge of His existence, the necessity of His essence, glorified is He, and the perfection of His attributes, Mighty and Majestic, and it mentions the great magnitude of His blessings and the grand favours of His bounty, Exalted is He, through His kindness to His servants, which is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 91, verse 9–10:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he has succeeded who purifies it﴾ is the response to the oath, according to what al-Jama'ah narrated from Qatadah, and al-Zajjaj and others went to this view. The omission of the lam (lam al-qasam) is frequent, especially when the speech is long, which calls for lightening, or for the lam being replaced by what stands in its place. The subject of ﴿zakkaha﴾ is the pronoun of "man" (man), and the object pronoun refers to the soul (nafs). The same applies to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he has failed who corrupts it﴾. The repetition of "qad" (indeed) in it serves to display the concern for affirming its content and to signal that the oath is essentially connected to it. Al-tazkiyah (purification) is growth (al-tanmiyah), and al-taddsiyah (corruption) is concealment (al-ikhfa'). The original form of dassa is dassasa, and the third of the identical letters was changed into a ya', then it was changed into an alif because it is vowelled and the letter before it is open. Some of them spoke in general terms and said: a letter of weakness (harf 'illah) was substituted for that, as they said in taqaddada, taqadda, and dassasa (for intensification) in dassa, meaning "concealed." The poet said:

"You buried Amr in the dust, so his widows became widowed orphans, neglected."

In al-Kashshaf: al-tazkiyah is growth and elevation, and al-taddsiyah is diminishment and concealment; that is: he has indeed won every desired thing and been saved from every disliked thing, who makes his soul grow and elevates it through piety, in knowledge and action; and he has indeed lost, who diminishes it and conceals it through wickedness
صفحة 144
in ignorance and transgression.

It is also permitted to interpret al-tazkiyah as purification from the filth of matter (al-hayula), and al-taddsiyah as concealment within it and being soiled by it. In any case, in the promise and the threat mentioned, together with His swearing by what He swore by, there is an indication of knowledge of His existence, the necessity of His essence, glorified is He, and the perfection of His attributes, Mighty and Majestic, and it mentions the great magnitude of His blessings and the grand favours of His bounty, Exalted is He, through His kindness to His servants, which is not hidden.

And His saying, ﴿Thamud denied [their messenger] because of their transgression﴾, is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) serving to confirm the content of His saying, ﴿and he has failed who buried it﴾. Al-Zamakhshari made His saying, ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾, and what follows, a continuation of His saying, ﴿and inspired it﴾, and what follows, by way of digression (istitrad). He refused that it should be the response to the oath (jawab al-qasam). He took the response as omitted, indicated by what has been said, as if it were said: "Allah will surely destroy the disbelievers of Makkah because they denied the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), just as He destroyed Thamud because they denied Salih (peace be upon him)." It was said in reply that this is because of what it entails of omitting the lam (of emphasis), and that it does not befit the inimitable composition (al-nazm al-mu'jiz) to make the lesser of the two perfections, namely purification (al-tazkiyah), the focus, since it is specific to the practical faculty, which is the aim of the oath, while the higher of the two, namely adornment with certain beliefs (al-tahliyah bil-aqa'id al-yaqiniyyah), which is the core of minds and the essence of what ages have churned out, is neglected. Even if it be granted that there is no such specificity, purification is the preliminary to adornment in both respects. As for omitting what the oath is about (al-muqsam 'alayhi), it is frequent and common, especially in the Mighty Book. It was objected that omitting the lam is frequent, especially when the sentence is long, and it is easier than omitting the whole sentence in its entirety; and he has mentioned it in ﴿Successful are the believers﴾. So what is the point of what has been said? And that purification is meant as growth (al-inma'), has no specificity, and is not a preliminary but an aim in itself. Even if it be granted, there is no barrier to giving attention to some preliminaries at times, since the aims depend upon them. So reflect.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said regarding ﴿and inspired it﴾: "obliged it (alzamaha)." al-Daylami related it from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

On this basis, al-Wahidi and the author of al-Matla' said: inspiration (al-ilham) is that He casts into the heart success (al-tawfiq) and abandonment (al-khidhlan). So when Allah, glorified is He, casts into the heart of a servant something of either, He has obliged him to that thing. What strengthens this is what al-Bukhari, Muslim and Abu Dawud related from Imran ibn Husayn: "Two men from Muzaynah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, tell us about what people do and strive for: is it something decreed for them and proceeding upon them from a destiny that has already passed, or is it concerning what they face with what their Prophet has brought them, and the proof is established against them?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'No, rather it is something decreed for them and proceeding upon them. The confirmation of that is in the Book of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ ﴿and inspired it its wickedness and its piety﴾.'"

This does not require that the servant's power and choice have no role at all in wickedness and piety, even if it is said that their ultimate source is Allah's creation of them. Otherwise His saying, ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ and so on, would contradict this, since the servant is made the doer of purification through piety and of corruption (al-tadsiyah) through wickedness. Attribution requires that the one attributed to have a role, and the aforementioned role suffices for it. The soundness of the attribution in truth to the servant does not depend on his act being creation (al-ijad). So the argument, from this attribution, that he is empowered to choose whatever he wills of wickedness and piety and to bring it into being with an independent power, against what the majority says, is nothing. Moreover, the hidden pronoun in ﴿purifies it﴾, and likewise in ﴿corrupts it﴾, refers to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, while the explicit pronoun referring to "man" (man) is taken as referring to the self (nafs). Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding this: Allah says: "He has succeeded who purified himself, whom Allah has purified and guided; and he has failed who corrupted himself, whom Allah has corrupted and led astray."

Rather, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami related from him that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say regarding His saying, ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾, the verse: 'The self has succeeded whom Allah has purified, and the self has failed whom Allah has deprived of all good.'"

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Muslim and al-Nasa'i related from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: 'O Allah, grant my self its piety, and purify it, You are the best to purify it, You are its Guardian and its Master.'"

In a narration of al-Tabarani and others from Ibn Abbas: that when he (peace be upon him) recited this verse, he would pause and say that.

Some of them, on the basis of these reports and the like, said that this is the preferred interpretation (al-mura'jjah). Sahib al-Insaf preferred it, on the ground that the pronouns in ﴿By the sky and He who built it﴾ and so on would be consistent with it, all referring to Allah, the Exalted; and that His saying, ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself (tazakka)﴾ fits it better, because tazakka is the reflexive (mutawa'ah) of zakka, so the meaning would be: "He has succeeded whom Allah has purified, so he purified himself." Nevertheless, despite all this, it should not be denied that the former meaning is the one that comes first to mind, and that what has been mentioned of reports is not explicit in determining the other meaning. Yes, it is explicit in refuting al-Zamakhshari's claim that it is a reversal by the Qadariyyah, by which he means the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah). So reflect.

Al-taghwa is a verbal noun (masdar) from al-tughyan, meaning exceeding the limit in disobedience. They distinguished between the noun and the adjective in the form fu'la of the roots from the letter ya': they changed the ya' to waw in the noun and left it unchanged in the adjective. So they said of the adjective: imra'ah sadya and khazya, and of the noun: taqwa and taghwa. Thus is it in al-Kashshaf and others. The words of al-Raghib indicate that taghaa and awaa, and it comes, where he said: it is said taghawtu and taghaytu, taghwanan and tughyanan, so do not be heedless. The ba' (in bi-tughyanaha), according to the majority, is causal (li-l-sababiyyah): i.e., she committed the denial because of her transgression, just as you say: "The wicked one wronged me by his audacity against Allah, the Exalted."

Al-Zamakhshari made it instrumental (li-l-isti'anah), and the matter is easy. It is also permitted that it be attached to the denial, in the sense: "She denied what she was threatened with by the tongue of her prophet, of the punishment that is characterized by transgression," i.e., exceeding the limit and excess. Punishment is described as tughyan in this sense, as in His saying, ﴿So they were destroyed by the tagiyah (the violent blast)﴾. It may also be described as taghwa by way of emphasis, as all verbal nouns are described thus, so there is no omitted modifier (mudaf mahdhuf) here. Al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Hammad ibn Salamah read: "tughwaha" with a damma on the ta', and it is also a verbal noun, like al-ruj'a and al-husna among the verbal nouns. However, it was said that the analogical form would be tughya, like suqya, because fu'la with a damma is not distinguished between noun and adjective; as if they deviated in it by changing the ya' to waw. You know that the waw, according to those who say taghawtu, is original (asliyyah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 91, verse 12:

﴿When he who was most wretched of them set off⦆ — "Idh" (when) is related either to "kadhdhabat" (rejected) or to "tughwa" (its transgression), and "inba' atha" (set off) is the intransitive form (mutawa'ah) of "ba'athahu," meaning "sent him," and the intended meaning is: when he went to hamstring the she-camel.

﴿Ashqaha﴾ means: the most wretched of Thamud, and he was Qudar ibn Salif. Or he and those who took it upon themselves together with him to hamstring her were two wretches, according to what al-Farra' said, or more than that. For the superlative form (af'al al-tafdil), when it is added to a definite noun, is suitable for the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine. The excess of their wretchedness over those other than them is because they personally carried out the hamstringing, while all of them shared in approving it, and because of other vile qualities that Allah Most High knows in them, which are beyond the vile qualities of those other than them.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 91, verse 13:**

﴿Then he said to them﴾: that is, to Thamud, or to the most wretched of them, according to what has been said. It is said that the intended meaning is plural, and this does not contradict it.

﴿And its drinking-turn﴾, as is not hidden. ﴿The Messenger of Allah﴾ is Salih, upon him be peace. He referred to him by the title of messengership to indicate the obligation of obeying him, and to show the extent of their insolence and their persistence in transgression. This is also the reason for the attribution of the she-camel to God, Most High, in His words: ﴿the she-camel of Allah﴾. It is in the accusative as a warning (tahdhir). Its condition is not the repetition of what is warned against, nor that it be warned against by what follows alone, so that it could be said that it is accusative by the implied verb "leave" or "beware" and not as a warning. Rather, its condition is that (repetition), or that it be conjoined to it, as here, according to what Makki stated. The speech is elliptical, meaning "beware of harming the she-camel of Allah," or the sense is so even if it is not expressed in the wording of the sentence. It has also been permitted that the implied verb is "glorify" or "adhere to" the she-camel of Allah, but this is nothing.

﴿And its drinking-turn﴾: that is, and beware of its drinking-turn, so do not obstruct it from its turn, nor monopolize the water against it. It has been said: the "wa" is for accompaniment, and the meaning is "leave the she-camel of Allah together with its drinking-turn, and do not come between the two," and this, as you see, is far-fetched.

Zayd ibn Ali read "ناقةُ اللَّهِ" with the nominative (raf'). It has been said: that is, your concern is the she-camel of Allah and its drinking-turn, so do not harm it, nor monopolize the water against it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 91, verse 14:

﴿فَكَذَّبُوهُ﴾ That is, they denied his warning, as is related by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you.﴾ So the denial was of a predicated report that was left implicit (khabar muqaddar). It is also permissible that the denial was of a report contained within the preceding cautionary command (al-amr al-tahdhiri), namely the report that punishment would descend if they did what he had warned them against. It has also been said that what he told them of the command, he said while relaying it from God, Exalted is He, as the reference to him, peace be upon him, by the title of Messenger indicates. The upshot is that he told them: "God, Exalted is He, has said: ﴿the she-camel of God, and her drinking-turn﴾." So the denial was of that, and this is an acceptable interpretation. ﴿فَعَقَرُوها﴾ That is, they slaughtered her or killed her. The plural pronoun refers to the most wretched (al-ashqa), and the plural is used although the act was by one person because all of them consented to his deed. Qatada said: "We have been told that he did not hamstring her until his young and old, male and female, followed him in it."

﴿فَدَمْدَمَ عَلَيْهِمْ رَبُّهُمْ﴾ So He overwhelmed them with punishment. They say: "dammama 'alayhi al-qabr," meaning he closed the grave over him. It is one of the forms in which the root's letters are repeated, so its measure is fa'fal (not fa'lal), from their saying: "naqatun madmumah," when fat covers and envelops it. In the Qamus (al-Qamus al-Muhit), it says: its meaning is that He completed the punishment upon them. A historian said: al-dam'amah is destruction by uprooting. In al-Sihah (Sihah al-Lughah), it says: "dammamtu al-shay'" means I stuck the thing to the ground and flattened it. Ibn al-Zubayr read: "fadahdama," with a ha' between the two dals, and the meaning is as stated above.

﴿بِذَنْبِهِمْ﴾ Because of their sin, the one that has been related. The explicit mention of this, although the fa' already indicates it, is to warn through the consequence of sin, so that every sinner may take heed.

﴿فَسَوّاها﴾ The pronoun refers to the destruction (al-damdamah) understood from "dammama." That is: He made the destruction equal among them, or He made it upon them equally, so that He spared none of them, neither small nor great. Or the pronoun refers to Thamud, and the feminine form is by consideration of the tribe, as in "taghwaha wa-ashqaha." The meaning is also what has been mentioned, or: He levelled them with the earth.

Page 146

﴿And He does not fear﴾, that is, the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿its consequence﴾, that is, its outcome and its aftermath, just as kings who punish fear the consequence and aftermath of what they do. This is an allegorical metaphor (istiʿāra tamthīliyya) for their humiliation and that they are abased before God, exalted is His majesty. The wāw is either circumstantial (wāw al-ḥāl) or resumptive (wāw al-istiʾnāf). It is also permitted that the pronoun in ﴿He does not fear﴾ refers to the Messenger, with the wāw being purely resumptive (wāw al-istiʾnāf), as is the apparent meaning: that is, the Messenger does not fear the consequence of this deed done to them, since he had warned them and cautioned them. Al-Suddi, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Muqatil, al-Zajjaj and Abu ʿAli said: the wāw is circumstantial, and the pronoun refers to "the most wretched of them" (ashqāhā), meaning he rose up to hamstring her, while he (the wretched one) does not fear the consequence of his act, because of his disbelief and tyranny. This view is much further from the context than what came before it.

Ubayy, al-Aʿraj, Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read "fa-lā yakhāfu" with a fāʾ, and it has also been read "wa-lam yakhaf" with a wāw and a jussive verb after lam. Concerning these people, there is disagreement: did they believe and then disbelieve, or did they never believe at all? The majority hold the latter view, while some hold that they believed and pledged allegiance to Ṣāliḥ for a period, then denied him and disbelieved, so they were destroyed for what is detailed in another place.

Shaykh al-Akbar Muḥyi al-Dīn, may his secret be sanctified, said in his Fuṣūṣ: They and the people of Lot, peace be upon him, have no salvation on the Day of Resurrection in any way, and others among the nations that denied and were destroyed in this world, such as the people of Noah, peace be upon him, are not equal to them. His words, may his secret be sanctified, have people who understand them, so return to them for understanding them, if you find them.

Some interpreters (ahl al-taʾwīl) mentioned that "the sun" (al-shams) is an indication of the Essence of the Necessarily Existent, glorified and exalted. "Its brightness" (ḍuḥāhā) is an indication of the Muhammadan Reality (al-Ḥaqīqa al-Muḥammadiyya). "The moon" (al-qamar) is an indication of the quiddity of the contingent (māhiyyat al-mumkin), which derives existence from the sun of the Essence. "The day" (al-nahār) is an indication of the world in all its kinds, through which the attributes of the beauty, majesty and perfection of the Essence became manifest. "The night" (al-layl) is an indication of the existence of the contingent kinds that are seen, which veil the True Existence in the eyes of those who are veiled. "The heaven" (al-samāʾ) is an indication of the world of intellect (ʿālam al-ʿaql). "The earth" (al-arḍ) is an indication of the world of bodies, and the soul (al-nafs) is known. "The she-camel of God" (nāqat Allāh) is an indication of the mount of longing that is connected to Him, glorified be He, and "its drink" (suqyāhā) is an indication of its drinking place from the spring of remembrance and reflection.

Another interpreter said: The sun is an indication of the True Existence, which is the very essence of the Necessary Existent, exalted be He. Thus it is more manifest than the sun: "God is the Light of the heavens and the earth." Our shaykh al-Bandanījī, may his secret be sanctified, said:

You are manifest, but you are not seen,
by eyes veiled by the dots (of the letters).

"Its brightness" is an indication of the first determinations (awwal al-taʿayyunāt), by whatever name you name it. "The moon" is an indication of the immutable entities (al-aʿyān al-thābita) poured out by the Most Holy Outpouring (al-Fayḍ al-Aqdas). Or "the sun" is an indication of the Essence, and "its brightness" is an indication of its existence, and the addition (al-iḍāfa) is for a conceptual distinction (al-taghāyur al-iʿtibārī). "The moon" is an indication of the first determinations, and "the day" is an indication of the contingents poured out by the Holy Outpouring. "The night" is an indication of them too, from the perspective of those who are veiled. Or "the day" is an indication of the attribute of beauty, and "the night" is an indication of the attribute of subjugation and majesty. "The heaven" is an indication of the world of subtlety (ʿālam al-laṭāfa), and the mention of "the soul" after "with" is due to its entry into this world, for the sake of attending to its matter. "The earth" is an indication of the world of density (ʿālam al-kathāfa). "The she-camel of God" is an indication of the path (al-ṭarīqa), and "its drink"

[p. 147]

is its drinking place from the spring of the Sharia. Something other than this has also been said. And God, exalted, is the Guide to the straight path.
